4158.dq: Makwe does not have lexical vowel length but does attest penultimate lengthening (PUL) at the end of a phonological phrase. A word‑final H tone that occurs in phrase‑final position regularly retracts to the second mora of the lengthened penultimate syllable
4158.dloc: p. 82, Section 2.1 'Verb-final H tones and phonological phrasing' (Persee page block whose header reads '82 Africana Linguistica 20 (2014)')
4158.prule: Two-tone (H/L) mora-counting tone language: every mora is H or L; verb stems carry no lexical tone and receive a tense-determined melodic H pattern (none, stem-final, stem-initial+stem-final, penult, stem-initial), plus optional pre-stem H from prefixes, followed by unbounded spreading / tone doubling. No word-stress rule is stated; the only prominence-like property is automatic penultimate lengthening at the end of the phonological phrase.
4158.srule: Not mentioned in Devos 2014 (Africana Linguistica 20: 81-99; whole article read, Sections 2-3 on tone, penultimate lengthening and melodic H): no secondary or rhythmic stress is described; the words 'stress', 'accent', 'secondary' do not occur.
4158.quote: The tone bearing unit in Makwe is the mora. Each mora has a definite value for tone, i. e. either H or L. Contour tones (falling and rising) are only found on dimoraic syllables in the penult of a phonological phrase and are analysed as combinations of H and L tones. Tone assignment as well as tone processes can be described by referring to H tones only. There is no evidence of downstep in Makwe, and when two H tones come together, they fuse (or a H deletes). As is the case for most zone P Bantu languages, Makwe has a predictable verb tone system (Odden 2003: 534‑535). It lacks lexical tone i…
4158.loc: p. 82, Section 2 'Background and complications' and Section 2.1 'Verb-final H tones and phonological phrasing' (Persee page block whose header reads '82 Africana Linguistica 20 (2014)')
4158.idn: Makwe; data: Data collected by the author for her descriptive grammar 'A grammar of Makwe (Palma, Mozambique)' (Devos 2008); dates of fieldwork not stated in the article; fn. 9 refers to 'the more northern part of the Makwe speaking area (which borders on the Chimaraba speaking area)'
4158.tone: The article never uses the words 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence' (a full-text search of the whole saved text, pp. 81-99: zero hits). It describes a two-tone system whose TBU is the mora, with contour tones only on the dimoraic (lengthened) penult of a phonological phrase, no downstep, H fusion, predictable (melodic) verb tone as in zone P Bantu, and penultimate lengthening (PUL) at the end of the phonological phrase with retraction of a phrase-final word-final H to the second mora of the lengthened penult. There is no explicit 'no stress' claim; the phrase-final PUL is the Eastern/Southern Bantu type that other authors treat as a stress correlate, but Devos does not say so for Makwe.

4162.prule: Iambic word structure: in any word of more than one syllable (sesquisyllable = presyllable + main syllable, including lexicalised compounds) stress falls on the final (main) syllable; the presyllable is unstressed, segmentally reduced and toneless. Monosyllables (the majority of the lexicon) carry their own tone.

4162.tone: Malieng is tonal: 'a tonation system with 5 tonal categories and 2 registers' (summary table, p. 113; ch. 5 tables), categories written A1/A2, B1/B2, C1/C2, D1/D2 etc., each correlated with pitch and phonation type. Stress is asserted in 5.8.6 and 5.9.2 alongside the tonal system; no instrumental stress study.

contra.head: The published descriptions contradict each other
contra.detail: Goulden 1996:109 (section 5.1.1, Kilenge dialect) states in passing that the noun prefix na- 'can take the regular antepenultimate stress, e.g. naa-pe "a paddle"'. Haywood 1996:147 (Maleu dialect) marks penultimate stress on every form he cites, including na-'roro and na-'vola, and states that when words are compounded stress shifts to the penultimate syllable; Thurston 1987:34, whose Kilenge data are Goulden's own 1982 recordings from the single speaker Talania (Thurston 1987:23, section 2.11), reports that for words pronounced in isolation stress is usually penultimate in all north-western New Britain languages, Kilenge (column 'Ki.' of table 2.17a) included.

4164.prule: Three reachable descriptions, none with a general rule plus a simplex data set for this language, and they do not agree. Haywood 1996 (Maleu/Lolo dialect, Pototpua village, data 1974-77) states only that compounds carry stress on the penultimate syllable; all 15 stress-marked forms on p. 147 (simplex 'avo, 'tia, 'ire, 'lua, na-'roro, na-'vola and nine compounds) are penultimate. Thurston 1987:34 (survey of the ten NWNB languages, Kilenge included as column 'Ki.' of table 2.17a and named two sentences earlier; his Kilenge data are Goulden's 1982 recordings from the single speaker Talania, p. 23, section 2.11) states that for words pronounced in isolation 'stress is usually penultimate in all languages', while running-speech stress is 'not worked out in detail'. Goulden 1996:109 (Kilenge dialect, the same 1982 single-speaker data plus Jill Grant's notes) states in passing, in the morphosyntax section, that the noun prefix na- 'can take the regular antepenultimate stress', single example naa-pe 'a paddle', on the very construction (na- + root) where Haywood's forms are penultimate (na-'roro, na-'vola). Two of three sources (one implicit, one hedged and group-level) point to penultimate; the third is an explicit contrary label from the same data set that Thurston summarised as penultimate. The record codes the better-supported position, penultimate (word-level, right edge, hedged by Thurston's 'usually'), and carries Goulden's antepenultimate remark as a dissenting description.

4165.dq: Primary stress in Malgana is typically assigned to the initial syllable of words, regardless of the numbers of syllables of individual items.
4165.dloc: §2.4 Stress, pp. 19-20 (pp. 32-33 of the ANU open-access file); vowel length: §2.1, pp. 12-13
4165.heavy: a syllable whose nucleus is a long (lengthened) vowel, aa or uu, in non-initial and non-final position ('a long vowel occurs in a non-initial syllable (excluding the word-final syllable)'); closed syllables play no role; the author doubts that length is phonemic ('there is no conclusive evidence that vowel length was contrastive in Malgana', p. 13)
4165.dflt: initial syllable takes primary stress; secondary stress on every second syllable to the right
4165.prule: Default: primary stress on the word-initial syllable whatever the word length. Override: a long (lengthened) vowel in a non-initial, non-final syllable attracts primary stress to itself (gathaagudu, ngathaanu, yanaangu); a word-final syllable never takes primary stress (wilyaa keeps initial stress).
4165.srule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables rightward from the primary-stressed initial syllable (rule ii; ['na.ngi."ya.nu]). 4167.srule: Secondary accent on the strong (second) syllable of each non-head iambic foot: quantity-insensitive iambs are assigned iteratively right to left from the right edge of the prosodic word, the final foot is the head foot (primary accent on the final syllable), and a leftover initial syllable is left unfooted, e.g. ni(gi.ˌta)(ʃmá.ˈtaa) 'he was pulled' (ex. 19), ni(giʔ.ˈʦi) 'it was bought' and ni.(gi.ˌta)(sma.ˈhaⁿ) 'it was wetted' (winning candidates of tableaux 24-25, p. 103; the losing four-syllable candidates (ni.ˌgi)(ta.ˈʦi) and (ni.ˌgi)(sma.ˈhaⁿ) show the same (σˌσ)(σˈσ) footing and are excluded by *(tV.ˈσ) and PRIORITY respectively, not by the foot-placement constraints). 4167.tone: Tonal: three level tones L/M/H, TBU = mora, all nine melodies attested on disyllables; contour tones only on long vowels, hence generally confined to the final (strong) syllable (p. 87). The source separates accent from tone but hedges on the phonetic correlate of accent (Marlett & Weathers 2018:23 'it is not clear that something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Me'phaa'; Carrasco Zúñiga 2012 proposes onset-consonant duration in the strong syllable; Herrera Zendejas 2018 claims accent goes to the syllable with the right-most highest tone, i.e. tone-conditioned). Cornelio Tiburcio 2022 (held, Ciénega del Sauce, an Acatepec-type variety, not tcf) tests and rejects the tone-conditioned hypothesis instrumentally: 'la posición tónica no está condicionada por los tonos... el acento consistentemente cae en la última sílaba de la palabra fonológica'.

evidence_works.detail: Instrumental study on the same community as the deciding source (Me'phaa Vátháá, 'centered around the town of Zilacayotitlán', p. 24 = zila1239). Material: careful (read) and reduced (retold-story, telephone) speech from 7 bilingual teachers raised in Zilacayotitlán or Tlapa, recorded on a TASCAM DR-05 at 44.1 kHz and force-aligned in Praat (speakers p. 31; secs. 2.3-2.4, pp. 33-48; '7 speakers', p. 70); linear mixed-effects models with random effects for subject, tone and vowel length (reported df t(3507) for duration, t(4367) for intensity, pp. 108-110). Measured: normalized F0 at vowel midpoint, vowel duration, F1/F2, and intensity at vowel midpoint, by syllable finality and by position (antepenult/penult/final). Found: no positional F0 or vowel-quality effect; 'For careful speech, final syllables are 150 ± 64 ms long, whereas non-final syllables are 124 ± 47 ms long. This means that in careful speech final syllables are 21% longer than non-final syllables' (p. 108; 46% in reduced speech, Table 3.22, p. 109); intensity 'There is no detectable difference in the careful speech, but there is an average difference of 1.3 dB between final and non-final syllables in reduced speech' (p. 110); 'intensity provides evidence for an iambic structure in Me'phaa Vátháá' (p. 110): both antepenult and penult differ significantly in intensity from the final syllable, and in reduced speech the antepenult is closer in intensity to the final syllable than the penult is (pp. 110-111, Table 3.24). Conclusion: 'Both duration and intensity point to accentual hypotheses that would make Me'phaa Vátháá accent either word-final or iambic' (p. 111). The author assumes the iambic/word-final analysis from Cline 2013, Herrera Zendejas (p.c.) and Marlett (p.c.) (p. 106) and does not decide between word-final and iambic; the ARPAbet stress digits used for alignment were all set to 1 'given the preliminary stage of our understanding' (p. 39).

4172.prule: Three-way weight (light CV; heavy CV: or CVC; superheavy CV:C or CVCC). A final superheavy syllable takes the stress (sa'bu:t, bar'ba:d); otherwise a disyllabic trochee is built at the right edge, so stress is penultimate ('challi:, pu'ra:na:, 'kala:), except that an LH foot is permitted only in disyllables, so LLH words stress the antepenult ('puria:). Stated for non-derived words, which are at most three syllables long.
4172.srule: Only case described: in words with two superheavy syllables (CV:C.CV:C, 'usually derived') both are stressed, primary on the first and secondary on the second ('sa:nˌd̪a:r 'splendid', 'ma:lˌd̪a:r 'rich'). No rhythmic or alternating secondary stress is described; every non-derived word (at most three syllables, one right-edge trochee) is transcribed with a single stress.

tn.quote: unlike the other languages within the Ubangian family which have two level tones, Manza possess three possible tone contrasts; high, mid and low. ... Every Manza syllable is associated with one of three level tones: low (L; indicated in this paper with an grave accent), mid (M; marked by a level line above the vowel), and high (H; indicated by an acute accent). ... analysis has shown that Manza does not have contour tones. What appears on the surface to be a contour tone is actually two level tones on adjacent vowels.
